prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B046 first after reading the opening ballots. It is the only shortlisted candidate where a single, sharply defined idea (magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms in a lattice, with Lamb-Dicke confinement) is paired with an unambiguous, quantitative experimental payoff: fractional uncertainty and stability at the low 10^-18 level, reproduced and exceeded across several independent national and university laboratories with different species. The attribution is the cleanest on the list: Katori for the concept and first demonstrations, Ye for taking the platform to record accuracy and stability and for the many-body clock work. The impact is not confined to timekeeping; it feeds the prospective redefinition of the second, clock-comparison tests of fundamental constants and dark-sector physics, and relativistic geodesy. Four of five members who ranked it placed it in their top three, and it is the one candidate that three members put first, so the committee support is broad across atomic physics and experimental colleagues rather than a single bloc.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the field has already been recognised twice nearby, with optical frequency combs in 2005 and the control of single trapped ions in 2012, so a sceptic can call lattice clocks an incremental refinement of precision spectroscopy rather than a new discovery. A second concern is timing: the SI second has not yet been redefined, and one can argue the committee should wait for that. A third is that the two-name configuration leaves out other strong contributors (Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and the Paris and Boulder clock groups), and I cannot settle those priority questions from the supplied record alone.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranked B046 first and raised whether the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes already cover it, and whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and think the overlap question is the real test. The 2005 prize honoured the comb as a tool and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems; neither honoured the idea that a neutral-atom ensemble can be interrogated in a magic-wavelength lattice so that motional and light shifts cancel, which is what moves stability by orders of magnitude through parallel interrogation. I do not think we should tie the prize to the formal redefinition. The physics is demonstrated by comparisons between independent clocks at the 10^-18 level now, and a prize awaiting a metrological committee decision would make our judgement depend on a different body's schedule.

responses.point: Goran Johansson put B046 sixth, with circuit QED first, and asked whether recognition should wait for the redefinition of the second and noted that other clock groups are not captured.
responses.response: I respectfully disagree on waiting, for the reason I gave Eva, but I accept the attribution point. I would not widen the prize beyond two names, because the magic-wavelength concept and the record-performance realisation are separable contributions with clear owners, and adding clock groups would dilute that. On his first choice, B006, I see real merit, but the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum effects in circuits sits very close, and the credited four names force an exclusion of Girvin or Blais that I find harder to defend than anything on B046.

responses.point: Mark Pearce also ranked B046 first and asked whether the committee should separate the original magic-wavelength proposal from later accuracy records and the 2005 comb contribution.
responses.response: I think they should be treated as one achievement with two owners rather than split into two parts. The proposal without the realisation is a good idea that was not yet a clock, and the records without the proposal would not exist. That is exactly why Katori and Ye are a coherent pair. I do not see a case for dividing the citation, and I would resist a configuration that dilutes it by adding a second field just to be inclusive.

responses.point: Bernhard Mehlig ranked B038 (topological insulators) first, arguing it is arguably overdue, mature, and well confirmed across HgTe, InAs/GaSb and 3D materials.
responses.response: B038 is a serious candidate and I rank it high on maturity, but I have two reservations that B046 does not share. First, the credited trio leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang for the HgTe prediction and the 3D materials work, so the chain from prediction to experiment is not captured by these three names; as Eva Olsson and Goran also noted, the credit is partial. Second, the 2016 prize on topological phases means the committee will be asked to distinguish this from TKNN-type physics. I keep it as a strong alternative, not a first choice.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson ranked B042 (magic-angle graphene) first, valuing a simple band-structure idea that predicted an interaction-dominated regime, and found the timing reasonable.
responses.response: I find the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction elegant and I accept that the correlated insulators are reproduced broadly. My hesitation is that the pairing mechanism is still unsettled and the experimental credit rests on one group while Cao, Fatemi and earlier continuum-model authors remain outside the names. I would be more comfortable with it in a few years, when the physical picture has consolidated. I do not read this as a judgement against the field, only that B046 is a finished result whose performance is already verified by direct comparison.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-ion prizes.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second, or treat the 10^-18 comparisons as sufficient evidence of maturity.

Whether early strontium lattice work by other groups (for example Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow) should change the two-name configuration; I rely on recollection of the achieved uncertainties rather than verified figures.
How strongly 2025 prize proximity should weigh against circuit QED (B006) compared with the overlap argument against B046.
statement.conflict_note: Possible indirect connection to flag: my profile records a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye's group is at JILA in Boulder, so I have a field and community proximity to the Boulder precision-spectroscopy environment, though the provided profile documents no collaboration, supervision or personal relationship with Ye or Katori. I also work in laser spectroscopy and coherent light-matter interaction, which gives me a field-proximity bias toward atomic-physics candidates (B046, B009). No other specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile; the committee may wish to decide on recusal regarding Ye.
